scenarios.description: General knowledge question — answered, not 'no record'
outputs:
Both are transport-layer protocols, but they trade off reliability against speed.

**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol)
- Connection-oriented — requires a handshake before data flows
- Guarantees delivery, ordering, and de-duplication; retransmits lost packets
- Flow control and congestion control built in
- Higher overhead and latency (20-byte minimum header)
- Used for HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, email, file transfer

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol)
- Connectionless — packets are simply fired off
- No delivery or ordering guarantees; lost packets stay lost unless the application handles it
- No congestion control by default
- Minimal overhead (8-byte header), much lower latency
- Used for DNS, VoIP, video streaming, gaming, QUIC/HTTP3

The practical rule: choose TCP when every byte must arrive intact, and UDP when timeliness matters more than completeness, or when you want to implement your own reliability layer on top.

outputs:
Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of merging developers' code changes into a shared mainline frequently — typically several times a day — with each merge automatically verified by a build and test suite.

The core elements:

- **Shared mainline** — everyone integrates against the same branch rather than working in long-lived isolation
- **Automated build** — every commit triggers a build, so breakages surface within minutes
- **Automated tests** — unit and integration tests run on each build to catch regressions
- **Fast feedback** — the pipeline should finish quickly enough that developers act on failures immediately
- **Fix-first culture** — a broken build takes priority over new work

The point is to avoid "integration hell", where changes diverge so far that merging becomes a large, risky exercise. Common tooling includes GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI and Buildkite.

CI is usually paired with continuous delivery (CD), which extends the pipeline to automatically prepare — and sometimes deploy — every passing build to production.
